label: TMUA 2022 · Paper 1 · Question 19

hints.title: Draw the sample space for the centre
hints.body: The centre is uniform over the given rectangle. Represent each possible centre as a point and think of the desired event as a region of that rectangle.
hints.recap: For a uniform point, probability is the relevant area divided by the whole available area.
hints.pitfall: Use the area of possible centre locations, not an area of either original circle.
hints.pause: Draw the rectangle and label its side lengths.

recall.reminder: For a uniformly chosen point, identify the available region and the event region, then compare their areas.

hints.title: Use the distance between centres
hints.body: For two circles to intersect, the centre distance must be at least the difference of their radii and at most their sum. Check these two bounds against the possible centre positions.
hints.recap: Internal and external tangency mark the distance boundaries for circle intersection.
hints.pitfall: One circle can lie strictly inside the other without the circumferences meeting.
hints.pause: Find which distance condition can fail inside the given rectangle.

recall.reminder: Internal and external circle contact occur when the centre distance equals the absolute difference or sum of the radii.

hints.title: Use the simpler complementary region
hints.body: Draw the centre positions where the circles do not meet. Check whether that region lies completely inside the rectangle, then subtract its area from the sample-space area.
hints.recap: A complementary region can be easier to measure than the required region.
hints.pitfall: Confirm containment before using a complete disk area.
hints.pause: Calculate both areas and form the probability of intersection.

recall.reminder: An event and its complement exhaust the sample space, so their probabilities sum to one.

solution:
The possible centres (a,b) fill a rectangle of area 4×6=24. Write d for the distance between centres. Circles of radii 5 and 4 intersect exactly when 1≤d≤9.

Throughout this rectangle, d≤22+32=13<9, so the only excluded positions have d<1. These form the unit disk centred at the origin, entirely inside the rectangle, with area π.

The required probability is therefore 1−π/24=(24−π)/24. The boundary corresponding to tangency has zero area, so including it does not change the probability. Answer F.
knowledgePattern: Use centre-distance intersection bounds and the area of the complementary disk
